about: Audit trail for proposals/approved-pairs.json: what an independent checker confirmed for every source (web search only; full texts could not be opened) and which claims were removed because they could not be confirmed.

pairs.rating_comment: 'high' is justified under the guide on two counts. First, serious harm is reported: Rivera 2012 describes hospital admission with PT >120 s and bleeding, Naranjo probable, and Zhang 2015 reports bleeding. Second, the Lam 2001 authors say the combination should be avoided, and the CUHK review (Ge 2014) grades lycium as a major-severity interaction. All human evidence is case reports, and the entry states this. rating_source 'team' is correct because no Hospital Authority rating was shown.
unsupported_claims_removed: Zhang 2015: 'INR 3.84 with haematuria' and 'Naranjo 6' were not seen in any search result (the abstract seen says only raised INR with bleeding and a probable interaction)
Zhang 2015: '3 patients, 6 g/day goji tea for 3 days, INR barely changed' was not found even by a targeted search; dropped from rating_reason and why_pro_en
Leung 2008: second INR value 3.86 not seen; 4.97 confirmed via secondary summary
MSKCC: exact wording 'juice, water and ethanol extracts' not seen; softened to 'extracts and juice'

sources_checked.label: Rivera 2012 Pharmacotherapy 32(3):e50-e53 (main source)
sources_checked.note: Search showed the PubMed record 22392461 under this exact title, plus an Ovid full-text URL carrying DOI 10.1002/j.1875-9114.2012.01018.x. The abstract text matches every claim: a 71-year-old woman on warfarin, admitted with a markedly raised, indeterminate INR (PT >120 s) after goji juice, with epistaxis, bruising and rectal bleeding. INR fell to 2.6 after phytonadione. Naranjo 6, probable. The main finding is fully supported.

sources_checked.label: Lam 2001 Ann Pharmacother 35:1199-1201
sources_checked.note: Authors, title, journal and pages confirmed. Content confirmed: a 61-year-old woman with INR 4.1 after several days of concentrated goji tea; weak in-vitro CYP2C9 inhibition (Ki 3.4 mg/mL); authors say other factors may explain it and that the combination should be avoided. I did not see PMID 11675844 or DOI 10.1345/aph.1Z442 directly in search output, but they match my knowledge of this record.

sources_checked.label: Leung 2008 Food Chem Toxicol 46(5):1860-1862 (Hong Kong)
sources_checked.note: Search confirmed the citation, DOI 10.1016/j.fct.2008.01.008 and PMID 18281140. Secondary sources tie the 2008 report to INR 4.97 after concentrated lycium herbal tea. One also describes an 80-year-old Chinese woman, and another notes a Hong Kong report. The second INR value (3.86) was not seen, so the fix says 'two episodes of raised INR (up to 4.97)'.

sources_checked.label: Zhang 2015 Toxicol Rep 2:1209-1212
sources_checked.note: Search confirmed the title, authors, volume/pages and DOI 10.1016/j.toxrep.2015.08.011. The abstract confirms a 65-year-old Chinese man on maintenance warfarin with raised INR and bleeding after goji wine, a 'probable' interaction (title), and the conclusion that large doses (>6-12 g) significantly enhance warfarin. Four details were not seen in any search result: INR 3.84, haematuria, Naranjo 6, and the 3-patient 6 g/day test with its INR values (a targeted search found nothing). These were softened or dropped. PMCID PMC5598317 and PMID 28962463 were not directly confirmed, so the DOI was added to the id.

sources_checked.label: Ge 2014 EBCAM 2014:957362 (CUHK)
sources_checked.note: The PMC3976951 record was confirmed, with DOI 10.1155/2014/957362 and the CUHK authors Ge, Zhang and Zuo. The text lists Lycium among nine herbs with a major-severity interaction with warfarin.

sources_checked.label: Tan & Lee 2021 Br J Clin Pharmacol 87(2):352-374
sources_checked.note: An NHS medicines-resources summary of this BJCP systematic review says staff should be aware of increased bleeding risk with warfarin when Chinese wolfberry is taken. Epistemonikos confirms the scope. The authors and DOI match my knowledge but were not printed in the search output.

sources_checked.label: MSKCC About Herbs: Lycium
sources_checked.note: The URL appeared in search results, but the page text was not shown. A secondary interaction summary says goji tincture/juice inhibits CYP2C9/2C19 in vitro, not confirmed in humans. That matches the claim, so the wording was softened to 'lycium extracts and juice'. Lam 2001 alone already supports the lay 'why' sentence.

owner_notes: Four published cases, one of them in Hong Kong, plus two reviews. The strongest of the 15.

pairs.rating_comment: 'Moderate' fits the guide. There is one human case with a clinically meaningful change (INR 5.31 with haematuria, and the INR returned to target once safflower was stopped), backed by rat data. No source describes major bleeding, admission or toxicity, and no authority says to avoid the combination. A search snippet also said a separate systematic review rates this pair as moderate on the basis of the single case. Keeping watch=true is reasonable because haematuria on warfarin could be read as 'high'. rating_source 'team' is correct; I saw no HA rating.
unsupported_claims_removed: why_pro_en: 'The review notes this exceeded the recommended daily amount of 10 g' did not appear in any snippet I saw; I removed it, and the matching phrase in rating_reason.
why_pro_en: 'safflower injection raised Cmax, t1/2 and AUC of both S- and R-warfarin' (2018 study): I only saw that it increased the anticoagulant effect and affected PK parameters, so I softened it.

why_en/why_zh: 'In animal studies, safflower on its own...' describes what injectable safflower products (safflower yellow for injection) did in rats, not oral honghua, so I narrowed it to 'rat studies using injectable safflower products'.
main_finding: the review says 'strongest evidence of potential interaction'; I added 'potential' (EN) and 潛在 (ZH).

sources_checked.label: Interaction between warfarin and Chinese herbal medicines. Singapore Med J 2015;56(1):11-18 (PMID 25640094; PMC4325561; DOI 10.11622/smedj.2015004)
sources_checked.note: Search results matched the smj.org.sg PDF (SMJ-56-11), PMC4325561, the dx.doi.org/10.11622/smedj.2015004 record and PMID 25640094 to this review. They confirm it covers 44 Chinese herbal products used in Singapore, that safflower is one of the 11 herbs with the 'strongest evidence of potential interaction', and the case: a 74-year-old on warfarin 1.25 mg/day with a therapeutic INR developed haematuria after 14 days of safflower 20 g (INR 5.31). On rechallenge with the same warfarin dose and no safflower, his INR was 1.64-2.57. A secondary site (hellopharmacist) independently describes the same 74-year-old, 20 g/day, 14-day case. I did not see the 'exceeded recommended 10 g daily' sentence myself, so I took it out of the entry.

sources_checked.label: Liu Y et al. Effects of safflower injection on the pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of warfarin in rats. Xenobiotica 2018;48(8):818-823
sources_checked.note: The PubMed record exists (PMID 28783419), and a Thieme reference list confirms the authors, journal, volume and pages. The summary I saw says safflower injection 'significantly increases the anticoagulant effect of warfarin by affecting its pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameters'. I did not see the specific claim that Cmax, t1/2 and AUC rose for both S- and R-warfarin, so I softened that wording. I added the PMID and switched the URL to PubMed; I could not check the DOI independently, but it fits.

sources_checked.label: Liu et al. Safflower yellow for injection enhances anti-coagulation of warfarin in rats. Xenobiotica 2024;54(2):75-82 (PMID 38445636; DOI 10.1080/00498254.2024.2326987)
sources_checked.note: Search results matched the PubMed 38445636 page and the tandfonline DOI page to this title. Rats received SYI 9 mg/kg IP plus oral warfarin. SYI alone or with warfarin significantly raised PT, INR and APTT. At steady dosing, R- and S-warfarin concentrations also rose. The authors conclude that SYI enhances warfarin's anticoagulation and slows its metabolism. I added pages 75-82 to the label.

owner_notes: One case report (INR 5.31 with blood in the urine, after 20 g a day for 14 days) plus rat studies.
The checker said 'High' could also be argued because of the bleeding. I kept 'Moderate' as checked.

pairs.rating_comment: 'low' fits the guide. For aspirin specifically, the evidence is lab/animal only (rat antiplatelet data, in vitro human platelets) and conflicting: the one rat combination study found no change to aspirin's pharmacokinetics or antiplatelet effect, apart from a further fall in TXB2. No human case reports or trials were found, and no authority 'avoid' statement. A safflower–warfarin human case exists (haematuria, INR 5.31, Singapore warfarin review), but it concerns warfarin, not aspirin, so it does not raise this pair. rating_source 'team' is correct because no HA rating is shown. watch=false is reasonable.
unsupported_claims_removed: effect_en/effect_zh: 'this has only been seen in lab and animal studies' implies that an extra effect on top of aspirin was actually seen in animals. The sources show safflower's own antiplatelet effect (rats; human platelets in vitro) and potentiation of clopidogrel in rats, not of aspirin. The only aspirin combination study (Shen 2024, rats) concluded the combination did not affect aspirin's antiplatelet effect. Reworded to say the evidence is lab/animal only, mixed, and that no reports in people were found.
main_finding_en: 'found that safflower reduces platelet clumping in rats'. A review reports other studies' findings, so 'found' changed to 'reported' (the ZH 指出 is already fine).

Lim et al.'s exact sentences (rat models, clopidogrel potentiation, GPIIb/IIIa ex vivo, 'cannot yet provide definitive proof') were not seen word for word in my searches. The core content (safflower covered with platelet-inhibition evidence; caution) was confirmed. why_pro_en already softens clopidogrel to 'possible potentiation', which is acceptable.

sources_checked.label: Lim JW et al. Traditional Chinese medicine: herb-drug interactions with aspirin. Singapore Med J 2018;59(5):230-239
sources_checked.note: Searches confirmed the article exists, with the journal, year, volume, issue, pages, DOI 10.11622/smedj.2018051 and PMC5966631 (URL matches). They also confirmed that it covers safflower (Carthamus tinctorius) as one of the four herbs with in vivo or clinical-trial evidence of platelet inhibition or aspirin interaction, that a fragment mentions caution with safflower and aspirin, and that a secondary review table cites Lim as saying safflower potentiates aspirin. I did not see the exact quoted sentences myself (rat models, clopidogrel, GPIIb/IIIa, 'cannot yet provide definitive proof'). They come from the proposer's smj.org.sg snippets and agree with what I did see. I did not see PMID 29796686 or the full author list directly, but both fit.

sources_checked.label: Lu PH et al. Safflower Extract Inhibits ADP-Induced Human Platelet Aggregation. Plants 2021;10(6):1192
sources_checked.note: Confirmed: Plants, June 2021, 10(6):1192, DOI 10.3390/plants10061192, PMC8230796 (URL matches). The abstract says safflower extract inhibited ADP-induced human platelet aggregation, and that hydroxysafflor yellow A, safflower yellow A and luteolin had the same effect. This was in vitro. The Tzu Chi affiliation fits the authors listed.

sources_checked.label: Shen DD, Yang ZH, Huang J, et al. 注射用红花黄色素对阿司匹林的药动学和抗凝作用的影响研究. J China Pharm Univ 2024;55(6):795-800
sources_checked.note: Confirmed: authors Shen Dandan, Yang Zhonghui, Huang Ji et al., J China Pharm Univ 2024, 55(6):795-800, DOI 10.11665/j.issn.1000-5048.2024031902 (URL matches). This rat study found no significant change in salicylic acid pharmacokinetics (P>0.05). TXB2 fell significantly in the combination group (P<0.01), 6-keto-PGF1α did not change, and liver and kidney markers did not change. The authors conclude the combination does not markedly change salicylic acid levels and does not affect aspirin's antiplatelet effect. The product is an injection, not oral safflower.

owner_notes: Lab and animal evidence only, and it is mixed. Low fits.

pairs.rating_comment: 'low' is correct under the guide: the evidence is animal and lab only, and it conflicts (Li & Wang found no added antithrombotic effect, while Lim's review says safflower potentiated clopidogrel). No human bleeding case or authority 'avoid' statement was found, so 'high' and 'moderate' are not justified. rating_source 'team' is correct because no HA rating was shown. watch=false is acceptable.
unsupported_claims_removed: effect_en/effect_zh 'In rats' / '大鼠研究': the Li & Wang abstract does not name the species; changed to 'In animal studies' / '動物研究'.

why_pro_en 'No human data found': Lim 2018 describes a human study of safflower injection added to aspirin + clopidogrel in ACS patients (efficacy, not bleeding); changed to 'No human reports of bleeding with this combination were found.' The same fix was made in rating_reason.
why_pro_en 'The authors note that in Asian countries clopidogrel is often used together with Danggui or Honghua': not seen in any search result; dropped.

why_pro_en 'Lim et al. ... suggesting safflower may potentiate clopidogrel': accurate as a quote, but it describes potentiation against thrombosis, which contradicts the primary study; reworded to state the conflict.
why_en 'makes blood slower to clot': the PT prolongation in Li & Wang was shown with clopidogrel, not for safflower alone; softened to 'showed anti-clotting effects'.
Lim and Lu author initials were not confirmed; labels shortened to 'et al.'

sources_checked.label: Li Y, Wang N. Antithrombotic effects of Danggui, Honghua and potential drug interaction with clopidogrel. J Ethnopharmacol 2010
sources_checked.note: PubMed record found at pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20176099 (J Ethnopharmacol 2010 Apr 21;128(3):623-8, DOI 10.1016/j.jep.2010.02.003). AGRIS lists the authors as Li Yanhong and Wang Ningsheng. The abstract confirms three experimental models, antithrombotic activity of Honghua against venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, no significant gain in clopidogrel's antithrombotic effect, and a significantly longer clopidogrel-induced tail bleeding time and PT. The species is not stated in the snippets I saw, so 'In rats' is unverified ('rodent'/'animal' is safe). I did not see the sentence 'in Asian countries clopidogrel is frequently used with Danggui or Honghua', so it was dropped.

sources_checked.label: Lim JW, et al. Traditional Chinese medicine: herb-drug interactions with aspirin. Singapore Med J 2018;59(5):230-239
sources_checked.note: PMID 29796686, PMCID PMC5966631 and DOI 10.11622/smedj.2018051 are confirmed. The full author list was not shown, so the label is shortened to 'Lim JW, et al.' The review says: 'In rat models, safflower has been found to display antiplatelet properties and potentiate clopidogrel in preventing thrombosis.' This conflicts with Li & Wang's finding of no added antithrombotic benefit, so the conflict is now stated. The review also mentions a human study in acute coronary syndrome patients where safflower injection was added to standard therapy including aspirin and clopidogrel, so the blanket line 'No human data found' was wrong.

sources_checked.label: Lu PH, et al. Safflower Extract Inhibits ADP-Induced Human Platelet Aggregation. Plants 2021;10(6):1192
sources_checked.note: PMC8230796 and DOI 10.3390/plants10061192 are confirmed (Plants, June 2021, Taipei Tzu Chi Hospital group). Safflower extract inhibited ADP-induced human platelet aggregation in vitro. The first author's initials were not shown, so the label is 'Lu et al.' It supports the mechanism only, not the drug interaction.

owner_notes: Animal and lab evidence only. Low fits.

pairs.rating_comment: 'low' with watch=true fits the guide. There is no human case report or human study showing a clinically meaningful change. The direct evidence is rat and cell data that conflict: Qian 2022 shows PT/INR rising, Yang 2024 shows warfarin weakened, and the 2009 study shows only non-significant PK trends. The only human data are observational and point to LESS bleeding (Hsu 2022), and Yang 2024 mentions an unquantified clinical observation of antagonism. No authority 'avoid' statement or HA rating was found, so rating_source 'team' is correct. watch=true is still justified because Qian 2022 showed PT/INR more than doubling in rats. The owner should know that SMJ 2015 counts notoginseng among the 11 herbs with the strongest evidence of potential interaction. Moderate would be a policy choice, not something the guide requires.
unsupported_claims_removed: Chin J Clin Pharmacol 2018 rat study and all its figures (INR 1.40 vs 2.49/3.34/4.46 at 48 h; rises in AUC, AUMC, MRT, t1/2 and Cmax): I could not confirm the article exists.

rating_reason: 'Three rat studies found a stronger warfarin effect (higher warfarin exposure, PT and INR)'. One of the three is unconfirmed (Chin J 2018). The 5-week study cited by SMJ found only non-significant trends and did not measure PT/INR. Only Qian 2022 showed a PT/INR rise.
why_pro: Eur J 2022 'CL/F by 10%, 23% and 33%'. Only the 33% high-dose figure was seen.
SMJ 2015 / main_finding: 'in rats, notoginseng raised warfarin levels'. The original 2009 study reports only a non-significant trend after IV injection. The wording is softened to 'in one rat study'.
effect_en/zh: 'some found sanqi made warfarin work more strongly (INR went up)'. After the unconfirmed Chin J 2018 is dropped, only one rat study shows an INR rise. Reworded.
rating_reason: the TRC 'Moderate' rating comes only from a search summary. Unconfirmed.
rating_reason: Hsu 2022 'does not name the anticoagulants'. Not checked. Reworded to 'results are not warfarin-specific'.
PMC4325561 as the PMC ID for the SMJ 2015 article was not confirmed. The DOI URL is used instead.

sources_checked.label: Singapore Med J 2015 (Interaction between warfarin and Chinese herbal medicines)
sources_checked.note: The search confirmed DOI 10.11622/smedj.2015004 and the abstract listing notoginseng among the 11 herbs with the 'strongest evidence'. I could not confirm PMC4325561 as this article's PMC ID, so the corrected entry uses the DOI URL. I did not see the notoginseng section text ('not located', and the 5-week rat study). The rat claim is backed by its original source, the 2009 Chin J Clin Pharmacol Ther study (IV PNS injection at 20 mg/kg/d for 5 weeks). That abstract says there were NO marked PK changes, only a TREND toward higher warfarin Tmax, t1/2 and AUC. The review's word 'increased' overstates this, and the corrected why_pro and rating_reason say so.

sources_checked.label: Eur J Drug Metab Pharmacokinet 2022 (PMID 35138605)
sources_checked.note: Confirmed as Qian et al., 'Effects and Mechanism of Action of Panax notoginseng Saponins on the Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin', 47(3):331-342, DOI 10.1007/s13318-022-00753-0. At 72 h, PT rose 110-126% and INR about 111-128% compared with warfarin alone. CL/F was 33% lower at the high dose, systemic exposure rose, and CYP3A4 expression was downregulated with no effect on CYP2C9. I could not confirm the 10% and 23% CL/F figures for the low and medium doses. A correction notice exists (PMID 35192182) that fixes figures.

sources_checked.label: Chin J Clin Pharmacol 2018 (三七對大鼠體內華法林的藥代動力學影響, ccj.pku.edu.cn aid=217233192)
sources_checked.note: Two searches (by Chinese title, and by keywords plus journal and year) did not find this article. Only the 2009 study came up. I could not confirm that it exists or that its INR figures (1.40 vs 2.49/3.34/4.46) are right, so it is dropped.

sources_checked.label: Yang et al. J Ginseng Res 2024 (PMID 39263307)
sources_checked.note: Confirmed as 48(5):494-503, PMC11385396, DOI 10.1016/j.jgr.2024.05.003. In SD rats and HepG2 cells, PNS sped up warfarin metabolism and reduced its efficacy, with higher NR1I3 and CYP2C9 and lower miR-214-3p. The authors report an unexpected clinical observation of antagonism.

sources_checked.label: Hsu et al. PLoS ONE 2022 (PMC9398017)
sources_checked.note: Confirmed: 'Concurrent use of Chinese herbal medicine and anticoagulants may reduce major bleeding events', DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0271965. It used the Taiwan NHIRD, 4,470 anticoagulant users matched 1:1 by propensity score. Panax notoginseng was among the single herbs linked to lower major bleeding. The design is observational, and the results are for anticoagulant users in general, not warfarin specifically.

sources_checked.label: Natural Medicines (TRC) consumer monograph: Panax notoginseng
sources_checked.note: The proposer never opened it and relied on a search summary. I did not see the 'Moderate' rating. A WebMD/TRC-type notoginseng monograph and HelloPharmacist mention animal data showing higher warfarin levels, PT and INR, but that is secondary. It is dropped as a source, and rating_reason now says the rating is unconfirmed.

owner_notes: The evidence points both ways: one rat study made warfarin stronger, another made it weaker.
A Taiwan database study in people found less bleeding, not more. Low with 'watch' is the checker's choice; Moderate would also be defensible.

pairs.rating_comment: 'Moderate' fits the guide. A meta-analysis of 20 RCTs in people found measurable changes on blood tests: more platelet inhibition, and PT and INR lengthened with PTS. Natural Medicines (TRC) separately rates aspirin with Panax notoginseng as Moderate ('Be cautious with this combination'). Two things argue against: no extra bleeding was found, and the INR change was small (WMD 0.22). The owner could reasonably choose 'low', as the entry already says. 'High' is not justified: no serious harm was reported and no authority says to avoid the combination. rating_source 'team' is correct because no HK Hospital Authority rating was shown.
unsupported_claims_removed: why_pro_en: Xie & Wang 2023 review statement ('saponins in P. notoginseng could enhance antiplatelet drug activity'). The source could not be found, so I removed it.
PMID 36569332 for Dai 2022 could not be confirmed, so I removed it (the PMC id and DOI are confirmed).

why_pro_en / rating_reason: the named preparations (Xuesaitong tablets and soft capsules, Xuesaitong and Xueshuantong injections, Sanqi Tongshu capsules) and 'some by injection' were not seen, so I generalised them to PNS/PTS saponin preparations.

why_en/why_zh: 'In rats, sanqi also helped more aspirin get into the blood', and in why_pro_en 'markedly increased salicylic acid Cmax ... attributed to increased GI absorption'. I could not see the rat paper's abstract (only its title), so I softened this to 'a rat study suggested sanqi may raise aspirin levels in the blood'. TRC backs up the direction.

sources_checked.label: Dai et al. Front Pharmacol 2022
sources_checked.note: Confirmed: Dai, Zhang, Jiang, Chen. Front Pharmacol 13:1015048, 7 Dec 2022. DOI and PMC9768032 match. Search results show 20 RCTs with 2,216 patients, CHD or ischaemic stroke, and a subgroup analysis by saponin type. PTS plus ASA prolonged PT (WMD 1.90) and PT-INR (WMD 0.22). The conclusion reads: stronger antiplatelet aggregation and anticoagulation 'without increasing bleeding risk, gastrointestinal side effects, and urticaria'. PMID 36569332 could not be confirmed (a search for the PMID returned nothing), so I removed it from the id. The named product list (Xuesaitong, Xueshuantong, Sanqi Tongshu) and 'some by injection' did not appear in my results, so I generalised them to PNS/PTS preparations.

sources_checked.label: J Chromatogr B 2017 (PNS and aspirin pharmacokinetics, rats)
sources_checked.note: Search found the title 'Effect of Panax notoginseng saponins on the pharmacokinetics of aspirin in rats' in J Chromatogr B 2017, in an index listing that also gave PubMed ID 27978468 (not added to the entry; the owner may want to check it). The PII prefix 1570-0232 is J Chromatogr B's ISSN, which fits. I could not see the abstract myself, so the Cmax and GI-absorption details are unverified. The direction (higher aspirin levels) is backed up by the TRC monograph. I softened the wording to 'suggested ... may raise' and added the full title to the label.

sources_checked.label: Sun et al. Molecules 2018
sources_checked.note: PMC6016969 is 'Inhibitory Influence of Panax notoginseng Saponins on Aspirin Hydrolysis in Human Intestinal Caco-2 Cells', Molecules 2018;23(2):455 (MDPI 1420-3049/23/2/455; ESTHER lists it as Sun_2018_Molecules_23). The title itself supports the claim that PNS inhibited aspirin hydrolysis in Caco-2 cells.

sources_checked.label: Xie & Wang. J Ethnopharmacol 2023 (PMID 36754189)
sources_checked.note: Two targeted searches (DOI/title and a key phrase) did not find this review, so its existence, PMID and quoted highlight are unverified. Not shown to be wrong, but under the 'verified only' rule I dropped it from sources and why_pro_en. The owner can re-add it after checking PubMed 36754189.

sources_checked.label: Natural Medicines (TRC) consumer monograph: Panax notoginseng
sources_checked.note: The vital.ly monograph=996 page came up in search. Its aspirin entry reads: 'Interaction Rating=Moderate Be cautious with this combination. Taking Panax notoginseng with aspirin might increase how much aspirin and Panax notoginseng is in the blood.' Confirmed, so I removed 'reportedly' from the rating_reason. This is not an HK HA rating, so rating_source stays 'team'.

owner_notes: Moderate rests on a review of 20 trials (stronger anti-clotting effect, no extra bleeding) and the Natural Medicines database.
The Natural Medicines page is hosted on a supplement shop's website (vital.ly), not the publisher's.
Because no extra bleeding was found, Low would also be reasonable.

pairs.rating_comment: The 'low' rating is right. The evidence is one rat pharmacokinetic study plus a review statement. I saw no human study, case report, bleeding event, or authority advice to avoid the combination. rating_source 'team' is correct because no HA rating was found. watch=true is reasonable since every finding points towards a stronger clopidogrel/antiplatelet effect, but the owner may choose watch=false. Ma 2018 contradicts itself (the abstract conclusion says CAMD fell, the results say it rose), which makes this weak evidence even weaker. That is one more reason not to go above 'low'.
unsupported_claims_removed: why_pro_en / why_en / why_zh: 'Molecular simulation suggested partial inhibition of CES1A' and 'may partly block a liver enzyme'. Ma 2018 reports lower hepatic CES1A mRNA and a simulated 'good interaction', not partial inhibition. The 'partially inhibited' wording seems to come from a different (FDDP) study. Reworded to 'appeared to reduce a liver enzyme'.

The entry left out that Ma 2018's own abstract conclusion says 'reduced plasma levels of active CAMD', which conflicts with its results (higher Cmax, AUC and MRT). A caution is now in why_pro_en and rating_reason.
J Stroke Cerebrovasc Dis 2022: the PII/URL and the quoted conclusion about platelet inhibition and the fibrinolytic pathway were not verified. Source and claim dropped.
why_pro_en: 'All data are preclinical' could not be checked for the studies behind Hu & Wang's pharmacodynamic claim. Replaced with 'No human study or case report was found.'

sources_checked.label: Ma et al. Evid Based Complement Alternat Med 2018
sources_checked.note: The title is 'The Herb-Drug Interaction of Clopidogrel and Xuesaitong Dispersible Tablet by Modulation of the Pharmacodynamics and Liver Carboxylesterase 1A Metabolism'. PMC6220743 and DOI 10.1155/2018/5651989 both match this paper (PMID 30498515). The design holds up: 30 male SD rats, clopidogrel 30 mg/kg alone or with XST 50 mg/kg, once daily for 30 days. The results say co-administration appreciably increased the Cmax, AUC and MRT of CAMD. Two problems. (1) The paper reports that hepatic CES1A mRNA expression fell and that molecular simulation showed a 'good interaction' with CES1A. The 'partially inhibited based on molecular simulation' wording seems to describe a different study, the one on Fufang Danshen Dripping Pills, so I reworded it. (2) The abstract's conclusion says the combination 'resulted in reduced plasma levels of active CAMD', which contradicts the paper's own results. The entry now carries a caution about this.

sources_checked.label: Hu & Wang. J Thromb Thrombolysis 2019
sources_checked.note: Confirmed: Hu Y, Wang J. J Thromb Thrombolysis. 2019 Oct;48(3):491-499, 'Interactions between clopidogrel and traditional Chinese medicine'. The DOI matches the Springer URL. The abstract says word for word: 'The pharmacodynamics of Panax notoginseng ... increased the antiplatelet activity compared with clopidogrel alone'. I could not see what kinds of studies (human or animal) this claim rests on.

sources_checked.label: J Stroke Cerebrovasc Dis 2022 (PNS with dual antiplatelet drugs, rats)
sources_checked.note: The only trace of this paper is a reference in WebMD's reference list: Wu Y, Wang W, Kou N, et al. 'Panax Notoginseng Saponins Combined with Dual Antiplatelet Drugs Potentiates Anti-Thrombotic Effect with Alleviated Gastric Injury in A Carotid Artery Thrombosis Rat Model', J Stroke Cerebrovasc Dis 2022;31(8):106597. Four searches failed to find the abstract, a PubMed record, or the PII S1052305722002919. The quoted sentence about the mechanism (platelet inhibition and the fibrinolytic pathway) could not be checked. Under the no-risk rule I dropped it. It was only supporting evidence.

I suggest leaving this as 'not in our database' for now.

pairs.rating_comment: 'low' with watch=true and rating_source 'team' can be defended under the guide, but it is borderline. On one side there is one small trial in healthy volunteers, it used a two-herb combination product, it measured only PK and a surrogate marker (thromboxane B2) with no bleeding outcomes, and the observational signal was not significant. On the other side, the authors themselves concluded there are 'significant pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions in healthy human subjects'. That could be read as a 'clinically meaningful change in human studies', which would make it moderate. The owner should make this call explicitly. Given the 'no risks' rule, the owner may prefer moderate. I did not find any Hospital Authority rating.
unsupported_claims_removed: why_en/why_zh (original): 'The researchers linked the change to higher aspirin levels...' is circular. In context 'the change' is the rise in aspirin levels, but the authors gave this cause for the thromboxane B2 drop, not for the aspirin rise. Reworded to name the thromboxane B2 drop.

COX mechanism (danshensu + aspirin + salicylic acid acting together on COX) is only partly verified. Separate rat/in vitro work (PMC4222847) suggests danshensu mainly inhibits COX-2 rather than COX-1, so the wording is softened to 'same type of body enzyme (COX)'.
Source 1 identifier: the ScienceDirect PII S0378874112004989 could not be matched to the article. Replaced with the confirmed PMID 22867637.

sources_checked.note: The ISPOR URL resolves to this exact title in search, and it is also indexed as Value in Health vol 16 issue 3, A271 (May 2013). pairs.rating_comment: 'low' with watch=true fits the guide. Evidence: the review says danshen inhibits CES1/CYP enzymes. One rat PK study found no change in clopidogrel exposure, while a multi-herb Danshen Yin rat study did change clopidogrel AUC, so the evidence conflicts. Two Taiwanese human database studies (2013 abstract, 2017 EBCAM paper) found no statistically significant rise in major bleeding with antiplatelets plus danshen or other prespecified Chinese medicines. No case report, no human PK study and no 'avoid' advice from an authority were found. A 2026 self-controlled case series (Ther Adv Drug Saf; PMC13169102) did find a strong danshen bleeding signal, but only with oral anticoagulants, not antiplatelets, so it does not raise this pair. That study is relevant to the danshen-warfarin entry. No HA rating was found, so rating_source 'team' is correct.
unsupported_claims_removed: why_en/why_zh call carboxylesterase 1 and the CYP450 enzymes 'liver enzymes' (肝臟酵素). The verified review sentence says only that danshen 'inhibited carboxylesterase 1 and most enzyme of cytochrome P450'. Softened to 'enzymes the body uses to process medicines'.

effect_en/effect_zh say 'Lab studies suggest...' (化驗室研究顯示), and rating_reason says 'in vitro'. The only verified source for this mechanism is the review's own statement; the underlying lab studies were not checked. Reworded to 'A review suggests...'.

rating_reason says 'No human interaction study or case report was found', but the same entry cites human observational data from Taiwan (antiplatelet users, bleeding admissions). Changed to 'No human pharmacokinetic study or case report was found', with the Taiwanese database studies described.

The quoted sentence does not say these enzymes are 'liver' enzymes, and it does not say the finding comes from lab studies.

sources_checked.note: The UMN Experts URL resolves to this title. It is Lee et al., Int J Pharm 2011. The authors concluded danshen has negligible potential for P-gp/CYP3A-mediated interactions. The label has no authors, journal or year, so I added them. I could not get a PMID. sources_checked.label: Tsai HH, Lin HW. ISPOR 18th Annual International Meeting abstract: Relationship between major bleeding and concurrent use of antiplatelet drugs with Chinese medications (Value Health 2013;16(3))

sources_checked.label: ADDED: Tsai et al. Uncertain Associations of Major Bleeding and Concurrent Use of Antiplatelet Agents and Chinese Medications: A Nested Case-Crossover Study. Evid Based Complement Alternat Med 2017:9417186 (PMC5558644; PMID 28831288)
sources_checked.note: The full peer-reviewed paper from the same Taiwanese group. It used 79,463 antiplatelet outpatients (aspirin, clopidogrel) and 1,209 bleeding admissions in 2012-2013. Danshen was one of the prespecified CMs. Concurrent use with the prespecified CMs did not significantly raise bleeding risk (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.51-1.95; OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.65-1.97). The estimates are pooled; I did not see a danshen-only OR. I added this source because it backs the 'not significant' claim more strongly than the conference abstract does.

pairs.rating_comment: Low is right. The only human evidence is a pharmacokinetic study in 6 healthy men, with a modest fall in exposure (AUC about 19%, Cmax about 27%). That is within the 'weak' range of exposure change, and the study had no lipid or clinical endpoints. A meta-analysis of human trials found better lipid results when Salvia miltiorrhiza was added to statins, which conflicts with any loss of effect. There are no reports of serious harm and no authority advice to avoid the combination. No Hospital Authority rating was shown, so rating_source 'team' is correct.
unsupported_claims_removed: why_en/why_zh say the researchers found less rosuvastatin was absorbed from the gut, with no mention of species. The gut-absorption finding came from the rat in situ intestinal model, not from the human volunteers. Fixed to say 'In rat experiments' (老鼠實驗).
why_pro_en says 'compared with placebo'. The comparison was rosuvastatin plus placebo against rosuvastatin plus tanjin. Fixed.
effect_en 'about a fifth to a quarter' slightly understates the 26.85% Cmax fall and does not match the ZH '約兩成至近三成'. Changed EN to 'roughly 20% to 27%'.
PMID 30962748 is confirmed only through a search summary. An exact-number search found nothing, but the PMC ID and the title match.

sources_checked.label: Yang J, et al. Pharmacokinetic Drug Interaction Between Rosuvastatin and Tanjin in Healthy Volunteers and Rats. Yonago Acta Med 2019;62(1):77-84
sources_checked.note: PMC6437397 confirmed by search. The first author is Jie Yang, the journal is Yonago Acta Medica 2019;62(1):77-84, and J-STAGE carries a matching DOI suffix. A search summary tied PMID 30962748 to this paper, but an exact-number search turned up nothing, so the PMID is confirmed only indirectly. Confirmed content: a randomised, single-blind, two-period crossover in 6 healthy men taking rosuvastatin with placebo or a tanjin-containing drug; Cmax down 26.85% and AUC0-12 down 19.43%; BCRP and OATP mRNA up in human lymphocytes; a rat in situ intestinal model placing the interaction at least in the small-intestine absorption phase, through enhanced efflux. The figure legend gives GMRs of AUC 0.77 and Cmax 0.70, which differ slightly from the abstract's percentages. The comparator is rosuvastatin plus placebo, not placebo alone.

pairs.rating_comment: 'low' is right. The only evidence is two rat pharmacokinetic studies, and they disagree: the multi-herb Danshen tablets lowered atorvastatin exposure, while danshensu alone raised it. They also used different products and doses. No human data or harm reports were found. rating_source 'team' is correct because no HA rating was found.

sources_checked.label: Effects of Danshen tablets on pharmacokinetics of atorvastatin calcium in rats and its potential mechanism. Pharm Biol 2018
sources_checked.note: Sun et al., Pharm Biol 2018;56(1):104-108, doi 10.1080/13880209.2018.1424209. The search returned PMC6130457 under this exact title. Rats got atorvastatin calcium 1 mg/kg with or without Danshen tablet (DST) pretreatment at 100 mg/kg. Cmax 23.87 vs 38.94 ng/mL, AUC0-t 41.01 vs 77.28 ng·h/mL and t1/2 1.91 vs 2.74 h, all p<0.05. The microsomal t1/2 dropped from 42.5 to 25.7, and the authors say this means faster metabolism. One caveat: the abstract calls DST 'a traditional Chinese multi-herbal formula', not danshen alone. The entry did not say this.

sources_checked.label: The Pharmacokinetic Effects and Drug-Drug Interaction of Atorvastatin With Danshensu in Rats (2025)
sources_checked.note: Mei et al., Int J Pharmacol 2025;21(8), doi 10.31083/IJP45265. The search found it at both the imrpress.com URL and journal.hep.com.cn. Design: 12 SD rats, danshensu 150 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks, then atorvastatin 10 mg/kg. Compared with controls, AUC, Cmax and t1/2 rose and CLz/F fell (p<0.05). This supports the 'opposite direction' claim. The label leaves out the journal and authors.

That is not direct evidence for this pair, so it does not justify raising the rating. watch=false is reasonable.

sources_checked.label: Zhang et al. Effects of Danshen tablets on pharmacokinetics of amlodipine in rats. Pharm Biol 2019;57(1):306-309 (PMC6507817)
sources_checked.note: Search confirms the title, journal, volume and pages (57(1):306-309), DOI 10.1080/13880209.2019.1604768, first author Haixia Zhang (Weifang Medical University), and the PMC6507817 URL. The design matches the entry: male SD rats, n=6, amlodipine 1 mg/kg with or without DST 100 mg/kg for 7 days, LC-MS/MS. pairs.rating_comment: 'Low' holds up under the guide. 'High' needs serious harm reported or an authority saying avoid. No bleeding case was found, the trial reported no significant bleeding, and Davis's Drug Guide is a nursing handbook rather than a regulator or the Hospital Authority. 'Moderate' needs a clinically meaningful change in human data, and the human RCT found none. 'none_reported' could technically be argued because a study found no interaction. The trial was small, short and in healthy volunteers, though, and a drug reference still warns against the combination, so 'low' is the cautious choice. The 'FOR THE OWNER' note correctly flags the Davis 'avoid' wording for the owner to decide. rating_source 'team' is correct because no Hospital Authority rating was found.
